topic: Internal course: Investigative Study of a Religious Practice
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Kosher laws separate meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils
items.claim: What are the main kashrut restrictions?

options.text: Permitted animals (mammals chewing cud with cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita) by a trained shochet; separation of meat and dairy; prohibitions including pork, shellfish and mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut, designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions, Denmark) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal-welfare grounds — a continuing source of dispute.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.

items.title: The Five Pillars of Islam have a strict canonical order
items.claim: What is the standard order of the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam?

options.text: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)
There is no fixed order; lists vary by region

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists them in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames the obligations differently — they recognise the practices but list them as part of the Ten Ancillaries (Furu al-Din), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong.

Zakat is typically 2.5% of accumulated wealth annually; Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn to sunset in Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice is not a generic 'doing good'. Islam has specific, ordered obligations with detailed theological rationale — exam answers that treat the Pillars as interchangeable miss the structure.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began over political succession in 632 CE
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two separate communities formed centuries apart in different countries

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632 CE without a clear successor, those who supported Abu Bakr (chosen as first caliph) became Sunni; those who held Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had been designated became Shia — entrenched after Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE

items.reveal:
Abu Bakr was chosen at Saqifah immediately after Muhammad's death. Umar (634-644), Uthman (644-656), then Ali (656-661) followed as the 'Rightly-Guided Caliphs'. Umar and Uthman were assassinated.

The First Fitna (civil war, 656-661) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. Husayn's grandfather was Muhammad; his death is mourned annually at Ashura.

Globally, around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Major religious traditions can be shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.
